## Purpose

This note applies the `riattrition` package to:

- Scacco, Alexandra, and Shana S. Warren. 2018. "Can Social Contact Reduce Prejudice and Discrimination? Evidence from a Field Experiment in Nigeria." *American Political Science Review* 112(3): 654-677.

## File Locations

```{r}
paper_pdf <- "/Users/yinghuizhou/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Projects/attrition application package/personal/paper/can-social-contact-reduce-prejudice-and-discrimination-evidence-from-a-field-experiment-in-nigeria.pdf"
replication_dir <- "/Users/yinghuizhou/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Projects/attrition application package/personal/paper/scacco_warren_replication"
# Package root relative to this file (analysis/..), so each copy of this
# document sources the R code that sits next to it.
package_dir <- normalizePath("..")

list(
  paper_pdf = paper_pdf,
  replication_dir = replication_dir,
  package_dir = package_dir
)
```

The replication files come from the APSR Dataverse
(https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/X8ZRVO): `Data_APSR.dta` (one row per respondent),
`Data_APSR_long.dta` (one row per respondent and round of the behavioral games),
and two Stata do-files.

## Summary of the Experiment

### Substantive question

Can positive, cooperative contact between members of groups in conflict reduce
prejudice (negative attitudes toward the other group) and discrimination
(treating members of the other group worse)? Observational studies struggle with
this question because prejudiced people may simply avoid contact with the other
group. The authors therefore randomize contact.

### Setting and sample

The study takes place in Kaduna, a city in northern Nigeria with a long history
of deadly Christian-Muslim riots (2000, 2002, 2011) and strong residential
segregation between the two religious groups.

- The authors selected the sixteen poorest neighborhoods among those that had
  experienced violence in the past, divided them into 46 enumeration areas, and
  randomly sampled households and respondents within them.
- The sample is restricted to young men aged 18-25, the group that typically
  takes part in riots.
- In total, 849 Christian and Muslim young men were interviewed in a baseline
  survey (August 2014).

### The intervention

The treatment is a free, 16-week computer-training course, the Urban Youth
Vocational Training program (UYVT), run from September to December 2014 with a
reputable local computer retailer.

- Classes met twice a week (four hours per week, 29 sessions) at a central site.
- Students worked in fixed pairs on a shared laptop throughout the course, with
  many partner activities (designing flyers, researching topics, presentations).
- The course contained **no** peace or anti-prejudice messaging; it was presented
  as a skills program, which reduces the risk that participants guess the purpose
  of the study.
- Students received a small transport stipend, and regular attenders entered a
  raffle for the course laptops (held after the endline survey).

### What exactly was randomized?

Randomization happened at three levels (Figure 1 of the paper):

1. **Program (UYVT vs. control).** 549 of the 849 men were invited to the course
   (Group A); the other 300 only took part in the surveys (Group B).
2. **Class type, among those invited.** About two-thirds were assigned to
   religiously mixed (heterogeneous) classes and one-third to single-religion
   (homogeneous) classes (Groups C and D). There were 30 class sections: 20
   heterogeneous and 10 homogeneous.
3. **Partner type, within heterogeneous classes.** Students were paired either with
   a partner of the same religion or of the other religion (Groups E and F).

The paper reports that class and partner assignment were stratified on prior
computer experience, educational attainment, and prior contact with the other
group (p. 659). It does not report stratification for the program assignment, and
the replication data contain no strata identifier.

All analyses in the paper are intent-to-treat (ITT). Compliance was 84%: of the 549
invited men, 5 declined at the baseline interview and 84 never attended a class.

### Outcomes

The endline survey (January 2015, four to six weeks after the course ended)
measured two kinds of outcomes.

**Prejudice (attitudes)** — three indices built from survey items that respondents
filled in privately on answer sheets (Table 1 of the paper). Each index is the
average of its items on a 1-5 scale, coded so that **higher values mean a more
positive view of the other religious group**:

- *Negative Attributes Index* (4 items): how well "arrogant", "unreasonable",
  "ungrateful", and "fanatical" describe the other group (reverse-coded).
- *Positive Attributes Index* (7 items): "friendly", "honest in business
  dealings", "responsible", "good citizens", "peaceful", "dependable",
  "intelligent in school".
- *Out-group Evaluation Index* (3 items): placement of the other group on
  five-point scales from lazy to hardworking, ignorant to worldly, and ungenerous
  to charitable.

**Discrimination (behavior)** — two games played over ten rounds each: a dictator
game (how much of ₦100 a respondent gives to another participant) and a
destruction game (how many of another participant's ₦50 notes a respondent
destroys, receiving ₦10 for each note destroyed). In each round the other participant is randomly drawn
from the respondent's own or the other religion.

### Attrition

Of the 849 baseline respondents, 795 were found for the endline survey, so 54
(6%) are missing all endline outcomes. Attrition was lower among men invited to
the course (4%) than in the control group (10%), because the study team could
update course participants' contact information during the course. The paper
reports no significant differences in attrition across class or partner types.

The prejudice indices have a second source of missingness: an index is missing
when too many of its items are unanswered. This is why Tables 2-4 of the paper use
716, 780, and 762 respondents rather than all 795 who were found.

### Main findings in the paper

- **Prejudice (Tables 2-4):** no treatment reduces prejudice. The program effect on
  the Negative Attributes Index is small and insignificant (0.07, SE 0.09), and the
  effects on the Positive Attributes and Out-group Evaluation indices are small and
  negative (both -0.11, SE 0.06, p < 0.10).
- **Discrimination (Tables 5-7):** being invited to the course makes respondents
  more generous to both groups, and being assigned to a heterogeneous class
  reduces discrimination in the dictator game relative to homogeneous classes.

## Application Strategy

We apply the package to **Tables 2-4, column (1)**: the program effect (UYVT
invitation vs. control) on each of the three prejudice indices in the full sample.

- **Continuous outcomes.** The three prejudice indices are averages of Likert
  items. (The game outcomes are counts of bills and are not used here.)
- **Binary treatment and design.** `assign_AvB` = 1 if invited to the course. The
  paper reports no stratification for this assignment, so we treat it as complete
  randomization of 549 out of 849 men.
- **Missing outcomes.** An index is missing either because the respondent was not
  found at endline or because too many of its items are unanswered. The package
  treats both as missing outcomes.
- **Missingness assumptions.** We report `general` (no assumption) and `mp`
  (monotone positive: being invited to the course never makes an outcome go
  missing that would otherwise be observed). The paper's explanation for lower
  attrition in the course group (updated contact information) points in the
  direction of `mp`. Because missingness here also includes unanswered items, `mp`
  requires that the invitation does not make anyone skip items they would
  otherwise answer, which is a stronger requirement than for attrition alone.

## Load Replication Data

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(haven)
library(knitr)

# Display helpers. Rates are stored as proportions and shown as percentages.
fmt3 <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 3, format = "f")
fmt_n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
fmt_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
# Table captions go through Markdown: escape "*" so Y*_i(0) keeps its star.
md_caption <- function(...) gsub("*", "\\*", paste(...), fixed = TRUE)

sw <- read_dta(file.path(replication_dir, "Data_APSR.dta"))
dim(sw)
```

The respondent-level file keeps all 849 baseline respondents, including the 54 who
were not found at endline. (The authors' own code drops them with
`keep if available == 2` before the analysis.) The variables we use are:

- `assign_AvB`: invited to the UYVT course (1) or control (0);
- `available`: 1 = baseline only (not found at endline), 2 = baseline and endline;
- `prejudice_negative_end`, `prejudice_positive_end`, `prejudice_eval_end`: the
  three prejudice indices (missing when the respondent was not found or too many
  items are unanswered);
- `religion`: 0 = Muslim, 1 = Christian.

```{r}
outcomes <- c(
  negative = "prejudice_negative_end",
  positive = "prejudice_positive_end",
  eval = "prejudice_eval_end"
)
outcome_labels <- c(
  negative = "Negative Attributes Index",
  positive = "Positive Attributes Index",
  eval = "Out-group Evaluation Index"
)

table(UYVT = sw$assign_AvB, found_at_endline = sw$available == 2)
```

## Attrition Summary

```{r}
# Share of respondents not found at endline, by arm.
attrition_by_arm <- sw %>%
  group_by(UYVT = assign_AvB) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    not_found = sum(available == 1),
    `not found (%)` = 100 * mean(available == 1)
  )
kable(attrition_by_arm, digits = 1)

# Share of respondents with a missing index (not found, or too many items
# unanswered), by arm.
missing_by_index <- data.frame(
  index = outcome_labels,
  missing_control = NA_real_,
  missing_uyvt = NA_real_
)
for (k in seq_along(outcomes)) {
  y <- sw[[outcomes[k]]]
  missing_by_index$missing_control[k] <- mean(is.na(y[sw$assign_AvB == 0]))
  missing_by_index$missing_uyvt[k] <- mean(is.na(y[sw$assign_AvB == 1]))
}
missing_by_index$difference <- missing_by_index$missing_uyvt - missing_by_index$missing_control

kable(
  data.frame(
    Index = missing_by_index$index,
    `Control (%)` = round(100 * missing_by_index$missing_control, 1),
    `UYVT (%)` = round(100 * missing_by_index$missing_uyvt, 1),
    `UYVT - control (pp)` = round(100 * missing_by_index$difference, 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Share of respondents with a missing index, by program assignment."
)
```

In every index, outcomes are missing less often in the course group than in the
control group, which is the pattern `mp` describes.

## Applying `ri_sharp_attrition()`

```{r}
nperm <- 10^4
```

All randomization p-values and confidence intervals below use 10^4 Monte Carlo
(MC) replications.

### Negative Attributes Index (Table 2, column 1)

```{r}
set.seed(20181)
negative_ri <- ri_sharp_attrition(
  Z = sw$assign_AvB,
  Y = sw$prejudice_negative_end,
  missing = "mp",
  nperm = nperm,
  outcome_name = "prejudice_negative_end"
)
negative_ri
```

### Positive Attributes Index (Table 3, column 1)

```{r}
set.seed(20182)
positive_ri <- ri_sharp_attrition(
  Z = sw$assign_AvB,
  Y = sw$prejudice_positive_end,
  missing = "mp",
  nperm = nperm,
  outcome_name = "prejudice_positive_end"
)
positive_ri
```

### Out-group Evaluation Index (Table 4, column 1)

```{r}
set.seed(20183)
eval_ri <- ri_sharp_attrition(
  Z = sw$assign_AvB,
  Y = sw$prejudice_eval_end,
  missing = "mp",
  nperm = nperm,
  outcome_name = "prejudice_eval_end"
)
eval_ri
```

## Visualizing the Negative Attributes Index

The histogram shows the randomization distribution of the Wilcoxon rank-sum
statistic under the sharp null of no effect, with the observed statistic marked.
Under `general`, missing outcomes in the course group are placed at the bottom and
missing outcomes in the control group at the top; under `mp`, fewer outcomes have
to be imputed in the least favorable way.

```{r}
set.seed(20181)
negative_general_plot <- plot_ri_test_stat(
  Z = sw$assign_AvB,
  Y = sw$prejudice_negative_end,
  analysis = "general",
  missing = "general",
  nperm = nperm
)
```

```{r}
set.seed(20181)
negative_mp_plot <- plot_ri_test_stat(
  Z = sw$assign_AvB,
  Y = sw$prejudice_negative_end,
  analysis = "mp",
  missing = "mp",
  nperm = nperm
)
```

## Comparison with the Paper

```{r}
# Column (1) of Tables 2-4 in the paper: OLS coefficient on UYVT with robust SE.
paper_coef <- c(negative = 0.07, positive = -0.11, eval = -0.11)
paper_se <- c(negative = 0.09, positive = 0.06, eval = 0.06)
paper_n <- c(negative = 716, positive = 780, eval = 762)

paper_table <- data.frame(
  Index = outcome_labels,
  `Paper: UYVT coef. (SE)` = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", paper_coef), " (", sprintf("%.2f", paper_se), ")"),
  `Paper N` = paper_n,
  `Difference in observed means (UYVT - control)` = NA_character_,
  `Observed N` = NA_integer_,
  check.names = FALSE
)
for (k in names(outcomes)) {
  y <- sw[[outcomes[k]]]
  observed <- !is.na(y)
  difference <- mean(y[observed & sw$assign_AvB == 1]) - mean(y[observed & sw$assign_AvB == 0])
  paper_table[k, "Difference in observed means (UYVT - control)"] <- fmt3(difference)
  paper_table[k, "Observed N"] <- sum(observed)
}
rownames(paper_table) <- NULL

kable(paper_table, align = c("l", rep("r", 4)))
```

The "Observed N" column reproduces the paper's sample sizes, and the differences
in observed means equal the paper's OLS coefficients up to rounding, since a
regression on a single treatment indicator is a difference in means. The paper's
tests use only these respondents (an implicit missing-at-random assumption). The
randomization tests instead keep all 849 randomized respondents and state the
assumption about missing outcomes explicitly.

**Direction of the test.** The p-value from `ri_sharp_attrition()` is one-sided:
it tests the sharp null of no effect against a *positive* effect (here: less
prejudice). The paper's estimates for the Positive Attributes and Out-group
Evaluation indices are negative, so we also report the one-sided p-value against
a negative effect. It is obtained by applying the package to -Y: a negative effect
on Y is a positive effect on -Y, and the missingness indicator does not change.

```{r}
# One-sided p-values against a negative effect: apply the package to -Y.
# No confidence intervals are needed here, so include_ci = FALSE.
less_results <- list()
for (k in names(outcomes)) {
  set.seed(20190)
  less_ri <- ri_sharp_attrition(
    Z = sw$assign_AvB,
    Y = -as.numeric(sw[[outcomes[k]]]),
    missing = "mp",
    nperm = nperm,
    include_ci = FALSE
  )
  less_results[[k]] <- less_ri$results
}

ri_results <- list(negative = negative_ri, positive = positive_ri, eval = eval_ri)

ri_table <- NULL
for (k in names(outcomes)) {
  for (assumption in c("general", "mp")) {
    greater_row <- ri_results[[k]]$results
    greater_row <- greater_row[greater_row$`Missingness assumption` == assumption, ]
    less_row <- less_results[[k]][less_results[[k]]$`Missingness assumption` == assumption, ]

    ri_table <- rbind(ri_table, data.frame(
      Index = outcome_labels[[k]],
      `Missingness assumption` = .ri_assumption_labels[[assumption]],
      `p-value, effect > 0` = .ri_pvalue(greater_row$`P-value`),
      `p-value, effect < 0` = .ri_pvalue(less_row$`P-value`),
      `95% CI for constant effect` = .ri_ci_text(greater_row$`CI lower`, greater_row$`CI upper`),
      check.names = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

kable(
  ri_table,
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = paste(
    "Randomization tests of the sharp null of no effect.",
    "The confidence intervals are affected by ties in the outcomes;",
    "see 'Ties and the confidence intervals' below."
  )
)
```

No test rejects the sharp null of no effect at the 5% level, in either direction
and under either assumption. This matches the paper's conclusion that the program
did not reduce prejudice. The paper's marginally significant negative estimates
(p < 0.10) for the Positive Attributes and Out-group Evaluation indices do not
survive once the missing outcomes are bounded, even under `mp`.

### Ties and the confidence intervals

The indices take few distinct values, so many respondents share the same value.
The Wilcoxon statistic in the package ranks tied values by their row order
(`ties.method = "first"`). Under the null of a constant effect c, the package
subtracts c from the treated outcomes. When c is exactly 0, tied treated and
control outcomes stay tied. When c is not 0, even by 0.001, every treated outcome
moves just below or just above all control outcomes it was tied with, and the
rank sum jumps.

The table below shows this for the Out-group Evaluation Index (15 distinct
values) under `mp`.

```{r}
# One-sided p-values for constant effects just below 0, at 0, and just above 0.
eval_y <- as.numeric(sw$prejudice_eval_end)
eval_z <- as.numeric(sw$assign_AvB)
shifts <- c(-0.001, 0, 0.001)

tie_check <- data.frame(
  `Constant effect c` = shifts,
  `p-value, effect > c` = NA_real_,
  `p-value, effect < c` = NA_real_,
  check.names = FALSE
)
for (i in seq_along(shifts)) {
  set.seed(20183)
  tie_check[i, 2] <- pval_sharp(eval_z, eval_y, c = shifts[i], missing = "mp", nperm = nperm)
  # Against a smaller effect: apply the test to -Y and -c.
  set.seed(20183)
  tie_check[i, 3] <- pval_sharp(eval_z, -eval_y, c = -shifts[i], missing = "mp", nperm = nperm)
}

kable(tie_check, digits = 3)
```

Every c other than exactly 0 is rejected, so the 95% interval under `mp`
collapses to [0, 0]. This does not mean the effect is estimated precisely. A
constant additive effect does not fit an outcome that only takes a few values, and
the interval reflects the ties rather than the information in the data. The
intervals for the other two indices end near multiples of the item scale (for
example 0.5 or 1/7) for the same reason. We therefore read the p-values at c = 0,
not the confidence intervals, for this application.

## Regression-based Attrition Diagnostics

These diagnostics follow the other application notes. Here `M = 1` means the
Negative Attributes Index is observed (as in Li, Sheng & Yu 2025); this index has
the most missing values. The covariates are baseline characteristics with few
missing values:

- `religion`: Christian (1) vs. Muslim (0);
- `a1_base`: age in years;
- `a4_hausa_base`: Hausa is the home language;
- `a16_simple_base`: educational attainment (0-3, recoded by the authors);
- `prior_computer_use`: prior computer use (1-3, recoded by the authors);
- `b4_base_simple`: relatively wealthy compared with the neighborhood.

```{r}
diag_covars <- c("religion", "a1_base", "a4_hausa_base", "a16_simple_base",
                 "prior_computer_use", "b4_base_simple")
diag_labels <- c(
  religion = "Christian",
  a1_base = "Age",
  a4_hausa_base = "Hausa home language",
  a16_simple_base = "Education (0-3)",
  prior_computer_use = "Prior computer use (1-3)",
  b4_base_simple = "Wealthier than neighborhood"
)

# zap_labels() turns the Stata-labelled columns into plain numbers.
diag_data <- zap_labels(sw[c("assign_AvB", "prejudice_negative_end", diag_covars)])
# Keep respondents with all six covariates recorded.
diag_data <- diag_data[complete.cases(diag_data[diag_covars]), ]
nrow(diag_data)

negative_ar <- attrition_regressions(
  M = as.integer(!is.na(diag_data$prejudice_negative_end)),
  Z = diag_data$assign_AvB,
  X = diag_data[diag_covars],
  labels = diag_labels
)
```

Respondents with a missing covariate are left out of these diagnostics, which
leaves `r fmt_n(nrow(diag_data))` of the 849 respondents.

### Regressions by experimental group

```{r}
kable(
  attrition_table(negative_ar, type = "group"),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = md_caption(
    "Negative Attributes Index: missingness regressions by program assignment.",
    attrition_table_note(negative_ar, type = "group")
  )
)
```

### Missingness regressions with and without interactions

```{r}
kable(
  attrition_table(negative_ar, type = "pooled"),
  align = c("l", "r", "r"),
  caption = md_caption(
    "Negative Attributes Index: missingness regressions.",
    attrition_table_note(negative_ar, type = "pooled")
  )
)
```

### Are covariates linked to differential attrition also prognostic of Y?

```{r}
negative_pc <- prognostic_check(
  Y = diag_data$prejudice_negative_end,
  Z = diag_data$assign_AvB,
  X = diag_data[diag_covars],
  labels = diag_labels
)

kable(
  prognostic_table(negative_pc, type = "side_by_side"),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = md_caption(
    "Negative Attributes Index: differential attrition and prognostic power by covariate.",
    prognostic_table_note(negative_pc, type = "side_by_side")
  )
)

kable(
  prognostic_table(negative_pc, type = "score"),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = md_caption(
    "Negative Attributes Index: treated-minus-control differences in predicted Y*(0) and in observed Y.",
    prognostic_table_note(negative_pc, type = "score")
  )
)
```

## Notes and Limitations

- **Other comparisons.** The paper's main comparison of interest is heterogeneous
  vs. homogeneous classes (`assign_CvD`, columns 4-6). That assignment was
  stratified, but the replication data do not contain the strata, so a
  randomization test could not reproduce the blocked design exactly. Attrition is
  also similar across class types (about 4% in each).
- **Ties.** The indices are averages of a few five-point items, so they take few
  distinct values (24, 48, and 15). Because the Wilcoxon statistic breaks ties by
  row order, the confidence intervals are not informative here (see above), and
  the p-values can change slightly if the rows are reordered.
- **Two kinds of missingness.** The analysis treats respondents who were not found
  and respondents who skipped too many items in the same way. The `mp` assumption
  must hold for both.
